---
title: "Weighted Average"
description: "An average in which each value contributes in proportion to an assigned weight."
term: "Weighted Average"
letter: "W"
category: "Mathematics"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

A weighted average gives some values more influence than others. For example,
the final course grade may give exams more weight than homework.

## Technical explanation

Given values $x_i$ and weights $w_i$, a normalized weighted average is
$\bar{x}_w=\frac{\sum_i w_i x_i}{\sum_i w_i}$ when the total weight is
nonzero. Weights may represent importance, frequency, confidence, or sampling
correction, but those meanings are not interchangeable. Negative weights or
weights that do not sum to one can change interpretation.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Weighted averages appear in metrics, ensemble predictions, loss functions, and
population estimates. Incorrectly chosen or normalized weights can bias
results, hide subgroup performance, or make comparisons misleading.

## How it works

Specify the meaning of each weight, multiply each value by its weight, sum the
products, and normalize by total weight if a conventional average is intended.
For probability mixtures, weights are commonly nonnegative and sum to one.

## Practical example

To aggregate per-class accuracy, weight each class accuracy by its number of
examples to obtain overall accuracy. The unweighted mean of class accuracies
answers a different question: performance on an equally weighted class.

## Common misconceptions

- A weighted average is not automatically fairer or more accurate; the
  weighting scheme defines whose outcomes matter more.
- Averaging metrics with different denominators may not reproduce the metric
  computed over all examples.
